#6159. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. But perhaps the most lovable feature is the private backyard, which has a pool, firepit, and full dining table, all surrounded by lush greenery and sleek appliances.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Observatory Park, The Robert and Judi Newman Center for the Performing Arts, University Hills Farmers Market, University of Denver

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: California king bed, flat-screen TV, immersive sound system, disco ball, LED lighting, faux-fire Malm fireplace, skyline views

Get groovy at this nostalgic studio apartment, which features an authentic disco ball and skyline views (including a peek at Coors Field, where the Colorado Rockies play) in the heart of Denver's Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood. Lucky for its guests, this spot is within walking distance of downtown Denver’s hottest entertainment, shopping, and dining outposts for a day or night out on the town. Plus, it’s equipped with all the amenities of your dreams, including a spacious California king bed, a 13-foot vintage couch, and a fully equipped kitchen for whipping up meals.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Coors Field, Commons Park, Little Man Ice Cream shop, Ball Arena, 16th Street Mall, Larimer Square, McGregor Square, Denver Union Station

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, fully equipped kitchen, private backyard, in-unit washer and dryer, kid-friendly amenities

You and your crew are in for a treat when staying at this charming, historic Boulder home. With original woodwork, colorful wallpaper, a fenced backyard, and three spacious bedrooms, guests here will enjoy a stylish stay.

Its location is the true star of the show: Right off Pearl Street, Boulder's happening hub of art, food, and entertainment venues, you'll be within walking distance from it all. Previous guests have raved about not having to rent a car when booking this base; even the airport bus takes you within three blocks of the address.

City: BoulderThings to do nearby: The Museum of Boulder, Pearl Street Mall, Boulder Theater, Pearl Street

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Rocky Mountain views, hot tub, outdoor kitchen with gas grill, firepit, Dobsonian telescope

Tucked on five private acres, this is a true mountain retreat in Bailey—a Colorado town less than an hour outside Denver, known for its quirky roadside attractions, outdoor recreation, and historic mountain charm. Dubbed “Skytrail Lodge,” this cabin fits right into the neighborhood.

The main living area is bright and welcoming, with floor-to-ceiling windows that bring the outside in. A big, comfy sofa anchors the living room, complemented by green and black accents that create an upscale, modern feel. Outside, lounge about on the deck and take in the incredible view of the Rocky Mountains. What better place to sip on your morning cup of joe, read a book, or indulge in an evening glass of wine?

City: BaileyThings to do nearby: Mount Bailey, Pine Valley Ranch Park, Brookside-McCurdy Trailhead, Crooked Top Mountain, Shawnee

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to ski resort, private hot tub, chef's kitchen, spacious design, smart TVs

Tucked in the storybook town of Cascade Village, you'll find a stay that exudes real mountain charm, with creature comforts to write home about. This Vail house is just a five-minute walk to Vail Ski Resort, with a free shuttle to Lionshead and Vail Village nearby. Meaning no matter the season—whether skiing or hiking—guests will have a convenient stay accompanied by the amenities that make an Airbnb great: a private, six-person hot tub; a fully equipped kitchen; en suite soaking tubs; private balcony access; and a laundry area.

Folks who stay here can cook up dinner on the grill or in the spacious kitchen, enjoy their meals in the eight-person dining area, play some groovy tunes on the Sonos speaker, and sip on a cup of coffee while looking out over the city and mountains. If you needed a sign to book a fun group adventure, consider this it.

City: VailThings to do nearby: Eagle Bahn Gondola, Lionshead Village, Vail Village, Ford Park, Betty Ford Alpine Gardens

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, wood-burning fireplace, shared hot tubs and heated pool, private patio

If you're looking for a stay in a mountain city that's as convenient as it is cozy, this Breckenridge condo is your solution. The renovated two-bedroom town house is designed for folks interested in exploring the downtown pubs, restaurants, and art-filled spaces—as well as the mountain trails, ski resorts, and beautiful natural surroundings.

Back at the rental, use the space to “ski, stroll, soak, and repeat,” as stated in the listing. Unwind around the crackling wood-burning fireplace, enjoy a home-cooked meal around the big dining table, stay in for a round of board games, or indulge in one of the condo's shared amenities: the heated pool, sauna, or one of the four hot tubs.

City: BreckenridgeThings to do nearby: Illinois Creek Trailhead, Carter Park and Pavilion, Breckenridge Brewery & Pub, South Main Street, QuickSilver SuperChair

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, wraparound deck, wood-burning fireplace, mountain views

Say hello to your next base for that upcoming group trip. This three-story timber lodge is all about space, convenience, and mountain fun. With a light-filled, open-concept kitchen and living room, you'll have some room to breathe. The floor-to-ceiling windows with sprawling mountain views and a wraparound deck make it even better. The home sits only 12 miles from Breckenridge, so it's drivable to the city's best hubs—from nature to dining—while also being tucked away enough to sprawl out and frolic.

Aside from the four queen bedrooms, there's a game room complete with a foosball table, vintage arcade games, table tennis, and more, making it a truly kid-friendly base.

City: AlmaThings to do nearby: Peaceful Valley Lodge, Wheeler Lake Winter Trailhead, Downtown Breckenridge, Montgomery Reservoir

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

With its ski-in/ski-out location and proximity to one of the lifts on Aspen Mountain, this is a stellar booking for snow chasers. But it's also a fantastic base for those heading to Aspen in the warmer months, thanks to its swanky year-round amenities, like a sprawling pool and hot tub with lounge chairs for relaxing or soaking up the sun.

City: AspenThings to do nearby: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort (one block to Lift 1A), Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bedsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, sauna, mountain views, wood-burning stove, design-forward interiors

This swanky cabin is ideal for those in need of a restorative nature trip. The cool cabin aesthetic extends throughout the open-concept kitchen, big windows, hot tub, and sauna—and the view of the sprawling mountain range is well appreciated.

The biggest peak you can see from the living room is the region's iconic La Plata, which is the fifth-highest in the Rockies. Mount Elbert, Colorado's highest peak, is at the back of the home, with one of its trailheads a few minutes down the road. Another big plus? The home sits just over a two-hour drive from Denver—making it a sweet weekend trip for Mile High City locals and a good road trip stop for those heading onward.

City: Twin LakesThings to do nearby: Rinker Peak, Independence Pass, Mount Elbert, Twin Lakes Village, Colorado Trail, Continental Divide Trail, Leadville

The lush Glenwood Springs is an underrated gem compared to its more frequented neighbors, Grand Junction and Moab. At this one-of-a-kind cabin, though, you'll likely question why it's taken you so long to plan a trip here in the first place.

Awe-inspiring canyon views await in every room through expansive windows, adding to the spot's light and airy feel. Each bedroom features a Tempur-Pedic bed and private deck access for true comfort and solitude. Indulge in the outdoor perks, too—there's a six-person hot tub, a firepit on the patio, and a four-person barrel sauna ready for post-adventure restoration. You'll also have prime access to the village's downtown square and its iconic hot springs.

City: Glenwood SpringsThings to do nearby: Colorado River, No Name Trailhead, Lookout Mountain, South Canyon Hot Springs, Horse Mountain, Hanging Lake Trailhead

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Mountain and forest views, private patio, bathtub, indoor fireplace, Wi-Fi

As one of Airbnb's most wishlisted properties, find this spruced-up, octagon-shaped tree house tucked away in the small mountain community of Cascade. It’s a scenic 15-minute drive from Colorado Springs, but you’ll find serenity easily among the tree house's natural surroundings. With floor-to-ceiling windows that look out to a little forest paradise, a wood-burning stove, a coffee and waffle maker, puzzles, games, and a smart TV, you'll never want to leave.

If you do plan to go out, you’re just five minutes away from Pikes Peak Highway, dotted with loads of gorgeous hiking trails, but you don’t have to leave your property to catch a glimpse of hummingbirds and other wildlife.

City: Cascade-Chipita ParkThings to do nearby: Ski and/or trails, scenic drives, Woodland Park, restaurants, reservoirs

This lofty town house—positioned (basically) right next to Garden of the Gods public park—is all about the views. The kitchen, living, and dining room all face the iconic Pikes Peak through a glass garage door. When open, it transforms the space into a picture-perfect indoor-outdoor area, complete with an overhanging balcony for taking it all in.

Two of the three spacious bedrooms sit on the home's ground level with shared bathroom space. There's also a separate “kids room,” complete with two twin beds—plus a trundle and space to hang out with a television (and a game system). You might not want to spend too much time at home, though: The home sits just a few blocks from Manitou Springs and Old Colorado City for sightseeing, restaurant trips, outdoor adventures, and more.

Just a one-hour drive from Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, this otherworldly home deserves a spot on your Colorado bucket list. It sits at the base of the Sangre de Cristo range, with mountain views by day and dark skies for stargazing at night. As one of the quirkiest picks on this list, this hobbit home has more creature comforts than appear at first glance. There's a kitchenette for meals at home, a dining table that seats four, and an in-unit washer and dryer. You'll also find an infrared sauna to relax in, as well as a firepit to cozy up around. #6158. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

#6157. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

#6156. 7 Airlines With The Largest Dreamliner Fleets In 2026

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner has become an important aircraft for airlines operating long-haul services, offering a family of twin-engine widebodies designed for different passenger capacities and route requirements. Since entering commercial service in 2011, the aircraft has been adopted by carriers around the world, with the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 offering different combinations of capacity and range. These three variants let airlines choose aircraft that better match their network strategies without relying on a single widebody configuration.

The world's largest Dreamliner operators demonstrate how extensively the aircraft family has been adopted across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America. This ranking compares seven airlines by their reported active Boeing 787 fleets, rather than combining aircraft already in service with future orders or scheduled flight volumes. Fleet registers can differ because of reporting dates and aircraft status, so the figures below should be read as reported late-2026 snapshots rather than permanently fixed totals.

Japan Airlines operates a substantial Boeing 787 Dreamliner fleet, with approximately 42 aircraft listed in the available register snapshot. The Japanese carrier uses the 787-8 and 787-9 across its network, giving it two capacity options within the same aircraft family. This combination supports different passenger needs without requiring the airline to operate every Dreamliner variant.

The 787-8 offers a smaller-capacity widebody option, while the 787-9 provides additional space for passengers and cargo. Operating both models gives Japan Airlines flexibility when planning services with different levels of demand, although aircraft assignments also depend on route length, scheduling, and operational requirements. The shared aircraft family provides commonality while retaining meaningful differences in passenger capacity.

Japan Airlines ranks seventh in this comparison because its reported fleet is smaller than those of the other six operators featured here. Its Dreamliners remain an important part of the airline's widebody operation, particularly as the carrier balances capacity across its network. The reported total represents a fleet-register snapshot, and should not be interpreted as the total number of Dreamliners Japan Airlines has operated throughout the aircraft program's history.

The airlines operating the most Boeing 787 flights in 2026 are based in the United States, Middle East, and Japan.

British Airways operates 43 active Boeing 787 Dreamliners, placing it sixth in this ranking. The aircraft form part of its long-haul fleet alongside other widebodies, including the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350. British Airways operates the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10, giving it access to all three main production variants of the Dreamliner family.

The 787-8 is the smallest member of the family, while the 787-9 offers additional passenger capacity and the 787-10 accommodates even more passengers. These differences give British Airways several aircraft configurations to consider when planning long-haul services with varying demand. Operating three variants allows the airline to select among different capacity options without depending exclusively on one Dreamliner model.

British Airways' reported fleet is slightly larger than Japan Airlines' in this comparison, but smaller than those of Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, American Airlines, ANA, and United Airlines. The Dreamliner complements the airline's other widebodies, each with its own role in the wider fleet. Its position here reflects reported active aircraft rather than additional Dreamliners that remain on order.

Etihad Airways operates 47 active Boeing 787 Dreamliners from its base in Abu Dhabi, placing it fifth among these seven airlines. Its fleet comprises the 787-9 and 787-10, which support international services across the carrier's network. The Dreamliner operates alongside other widebody aircraft, giving Etihad several aircraft options for routes with different passenger volumes and operating requirements.

The 787-9 makes up most of Etihad's Dreamliner fleet, with 37 active aircraft reported alongside ten examples of the larger 787-10. The 787-9 combines long-range capability with passenger capacity suited to a variety of international routes, while the 787-10 offers additional seating capacity. Together, these variants give the airline different options for matching aircraft size to route demand.

Etihad's 47 active Dreamliners put it ahead of Japan Airlines and British Airways, but behind Qatar Airways and the three largest fleets in this ranking. Its fleet composition shows a clear preference for the 787-9, while the 787-10 provides a higher-capacity option within the same family. The reported active-aircraft count is separate from scheduled flight totals, which measure planned operations rather than the number of aircraft operated.

Qatar Airways operates 61 active Boeing 787 Dreamliners as part of its international network from Doha. The airline uses the 787-8 and 787-9, providing two capacity options within its widebody fleet. These aircraft complement other types, including the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350, giving Qatar Airways a broader range of aircraft for different routes and passenger requirements.

The 787-8 provides a smaller-capacity configuration, while the 787-9 offers additional space for passengers and cargo within the same aircraft family. Qatar Airways' reported fleet includes 32 active 787-8s and 29 active 787-9s, with another 787-9 listed as on order in the available register. This mix gives the airline flexibility when assigning aircraft across its international network.

In May 2025, Qatar Airways announced an agreement covering up to 210 widebody aircraft, including 130 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Boeing described the 787 portion as the largest Dreamliner order in its history, underlining the scale of the airline's future fleet plans. These aircraft are not part of the current active fleet total, however, and should only be counted as they are delivered and enter service.

In 2025, Dreamliners flew over 16,000 flights from the airline’s five busiest Boeing 787 hubs.

American Airlines operates a large Boeing 787 Dreamliner fleet, with 67 active aircraft listed in the available register snapshot. The aircraft support the carrier's international network and form part of its wider fleet of Boeing widebodies. American operates the 787-8 and 787-9, giving it two capacity options within the Dreamliner family for routes with different passenger and cargo requirements.

The 787-8 provides a lower-capacity widebody option, while the 787-9 offers additional room for passengers and cargo. Operating both variants gives American Airlines flexibility when planning long-haul services with different passenger demand and operational requirements. The airline does not operate the 787-10, so its Dreamliner fleet is built around these two models.

American's 67 active Dreamliners place it third in this ranking, behind ANA and United Airlines but ahead of Qatar Airways and the other operators listed below it. Cirium schedule data for 2026 also listed 33,192 scheduled Dreamliner round trips for American, equivalent to 66,384 one-way flight sectors. Those figures describe planned services rather than flights confirmed as completed, making them a separate measure from the airline's active aircraft total.

All Nippon Airways, widely known as ANA, was the launch customer for the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, placing an order for 50 aircraft in April 2004. The airline received its first Dreamliner in 2011, helping introduce the aircraft into commercial service. ANA's early involvement in the program and its continued use of the type make it one of the most prominent Dreamliner operators worldwide.

ANA operates the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10, giving it a range of passenger capacities within the same aircraft family. The 787-9 forms a substantial part of the fleet, while the 787-8 and 787-10 provide additional options for different capacity requirements. This combination allows the airline to deploy the Dreamliner across its network without relying on a single aircraft configuration.

ANA was long associated with the position of the world's largest Dreamliner operator, but recent reporting in October 2026 puts its fleet at 92 aircraft, behind United Airlines' 96. The Boeing 787 Register's general operator table has displayed a lower figure, illustrating how reported totals can differ by source and update date. For this ranking, the 92-aircraft figure follows the late-October report, while the discrepancy should be checked against the publication's chosen fleet-data source before the article goes live.

United Airlines has overtaken ANA as the world's largest Boeing 787 operator, with further Dreamliner expansion planned.

United Airlines leads this ranking with 96 active Boeing 787 Dreamliners, according to its individual fleet listing in the Boeing 787 Register. The aircraft operate across the carrier's extensive network, providing widebody capacity for domestic and international services. United also has additional Dreamliners on order, but those aircraft are separate from the active fleet total used here.

United operates all three main Dreamliner variants, the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10, giving it several aircraft configurations for different capacity requirements. The 787-9 is the largest part of its fleet, with 63 active aircraft, while the airline also operates 12 787-8s and 21 787-10s. This mix gives United a range of passenger capacities within a common aircraft family.

United's 96 active aircraft put it ahead of ANA, American Airlines, Qatar Airways, Etihad Airways, British Airways, and Japan Airlines in this comparison. Its leading position reflects aircraft currently listed as active, rather than the number of Dreamliners ordered or expected in future deliveries. As United receives additional aircraft and other airlines expand their fleets, the ranking may change, making it important to distinguish active aircraft from future orders.

#6155. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6154. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

For anyone looking for a fun weekend getaway, Nashville almost always makes the short list of options. And for good reason, it’s a city packed with character, history, live music and excellent food.

I was lucky enough to grow up in the Nashville area, so the world of the Ryman Auditorium, the Grand Ole Opry and even excellent airport musicians will always feel like home. I recently went back for a short trip, and while I was there, I made sure to hit some of my favorite food spots — and check out some new ones while I was at it.

If you have Nashville on your list, don’t miss these favorite eateries. And for any food-focused trip, a card that earns on dining is worth having, like the Navy Federal Flagship Premier Visa Signature®. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases and 4 points per dollar on travel purchases, a strong combination for a trip like this, and all for just a $95 annual fee.

If you need a great travel and dining card, now is the perfect time to add the Flagship Premier card to your wallet. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 50,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 in the first 90 days from account opening. Offer ends Jan. 3, 2027.

Here’s how to use the card to make your food-focused weekend trip to Nashville even better.

I live on the West Coast now, so my go-to flight is usually a nonstop on Alaska Airlines, but I sometimes opt for another airline. With the Flagship Premier card earning on a wide range of travel purchases, I can compare prices and book whichever flight makes the most sense — no loyalty to one airline or travel portal required.

The Flagship Premier card can also help you save on your flight to Nashville with its $100 annual airline credit, which offsets the cost and gives you more flexibility when booking.

And when you’re at the airport, you’ll be thankful for Flagship Premier’s statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck® to help you zip through security.

When it was time to choose my hotel, I knew I wanted to stay at The Thompson Nashville. It’s in the Gulch, making it within walking distance of many of my favorite dining and shopping spots.

Regardless of which hotel you choose, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar when you book on your Flagship Premier card. That means you’re free to pick whichever hotel you want, without worrying about staying within a single brand or portal to earn bonus points.

Flagship Premier tip: Earn 4 points per dollar on a wide range of travel spending — not just hotels and airfare. Ground transportation counts too, whether you’re in a rental car, on public transport or using rideshare services.

Nashville has quite the dining scene, and the list of standout spots seems to grow every day. To make sure I fit in as much as possible, I turned one day into my own food crawl, with a combination of old favorites and a few newer ones.

For a food-focused trip like this, the Flagship Premier card earns where it matters most. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, so you’ll earn bonus points wherever your taste buds take you.

Since moving away from Nashville, I’ve come to realize that few places make a better chicken biscuit than Biscuit Love. Biscuit Love is an iconic Nashville staple, but it was new to me, so I knew it would make the list when I saw it around the corner from my hotel.

It absolutely lived up to the hype. From the fun southern and country-music themed decor to the food worth writing home about, Biscuit Love has landed a permanent spot on my list of favorite Nashville eateries.

The menu spans southern staples like biscuits and gravy and shrimp and grits, as well as lighter options like oatmeal and omelets. I knew I wanted to try their Princess biscuit, a buttermilk biscuit topped with fried Nashville “Hot Chicken” and homemade pickles. I also added the summer special Sunshine latte to my order — an iced latte with tangerine, cinnamon and vanilla and topped with housemade salted honey cold foam. And, of course, a side of bacon.

The entire meal was excellent. The chicken was perfectly fried, the biscuit light and fluffy and the pickles delightfully tangy. And the sunshine latte, I discovered, is a favorite for a reason. It was the perfect morning treat to start the day.

After such a big breakfast, I had to wait a while before I could even think about lunch. But when the time finally came, I knew I was headed to Ladybird Taco for my favorite tacos in Nashville.

A location a few blocks from my hotel made it an easy walk. Wanting to pace myself a bit this time, I opted for just one brisket taco and a side of chips and queso.

While I haven’t been to all the taco joints Nashville has to offer, the Austin-inspired menu at Ladybird has been my favorite for years, and I was thrilled to be back for a taste. If you happen to be there for breakfast, be sure to check out their breakfast tacos and Crema coffee — I’m always surprised at how well their coffee and queso go together.

After lunch, I was ready for an afternoon pick-me-up. Living on the West Coast has raised my coffee standards pretty high, but Barista Parlor never disappoints.

I popped in for an iced whiskey-caramel latte as a post-lunch treat to keep me going through the rest of my day in Nashville.

While Jeni’s isn’t Nashville-exclusive, it's only available in select cities and is a spot I make sure to visit every time I’m in town for its creative, seasonal flavors. I originally went in for my favorite — Brambleberry Crisp — but was tempted by the new fall lineup on the menu, which included Pumpkin with Brown Sugar Blondies.

I took a risk and ordered a half scoop of each and was delighted to discover that they pair beautifully. (Just learn from my mistakes and be sure to eat your ice cream quickly if you happen to be there during a heat wave.)

To close out my food crawl day, I headed to The Optimist, a seafood restaurant from chef and restaurateur Ford Fry that was new to me. I love every restaurant of his I’ve been to, and so many of my friends had raved about this one that I wanted to see if it lived up to the hype.

One of my good friends joined me, and we set out to try some of the hottest dishes.

While we surveyed the menu, our server brought rolls for us to enjoy. They were soft and fluffy — and the perfect thing to snack on while deciding.

Per our server’s recommendations, we landed on the Alabama Blue Crab dip and a half dozen oysters, which were both an excellent start to the meal (and complement to our Champagne).

We then moved to the spicy kale salad, which was aptly named. While delicious, it was too spicy for either of us to enjoy more than a few bites.

For our main dish, we ordered the Crumbed Halibut (with brown butter, parsley and charred lemon) and a side of “Proper ‘Chips’” (with malt vinegar aioli). The Halibut was crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, and the brown butter made it sing. The fries were equally well-executed, and the aioli took them to the next level.

The verdict: The Optimist lives up to the hype. I’ll definitely prioritize going back the next time I’m in town.

Flagship Premier Tip: Earn 3 points per dollar on all dining, making this a great card to have handy when exploring local cuisines — from a nearby coffee stop to the splashiest seafood dinner in town.

A card that earns on both travel and dining makes a trip like this Nashville weekend a breeze, and that’s exactly what the Flagship Premier card does.

With the card, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar on your travel purchases — from hotels and flights to transportation while you’re there, without having to deal with booking through a travel portal.

The $100 annual airline credit and up to $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit (once every four years) take the edge off both the cost of flying and the airport experience.

No one likes to juggle multiple cards while traveling, and the Flagship Premier card keeps things simple. With 4 points per dollar on travel and 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, one card covers the two categories that matter most on a trip like this.

Plus, there are no limits on the rewards you can earn (other than your stomach at the end of your food crawl).

If you haven’t been to Nashville lately, be sure to add it to your list — along with these excellent food spots while you’re there.

And wherever your next trip takes you, the Navy Federal Flagship Premier card is worth bringing along, especially for trips centered on food and travel. Between the travel credits and elevated earning rates, it’s the perfect card for any trip.

#6151. JetBlue Cancels 19 Routes From Florida: See Full List Now

For obvious reasons, Florida continues to play a critical role in JetBlue's network. Between November and next summer, the latest Cirium Diio data shows that the carrier has far more flights touching the Sunshine State than anywhere else.

Ten markets in Florida are served: Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Fort Myers, Jacksonville, Key West, Orlando, Sarasota, Tampa, Vero Beach, and West Palm Beach. Depending on the specific month, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) is now JetBlue's most-served airport across its entire network, surpassing New York JFK.

Comparing the airline's domestic Florida network between January and October 2026 with what's scheduled from November 2026 onwards shows that these routes have all ended. They include several routes that were only served for Spring Break, including Bozeman, Denver, Portland, Reno, and Salt Lake City to FLL. As flights do not return in 2027, the airline was clearly underwhelmed by the performance relative to what else it could do with the aircraft.

Five weekly A320 (only 10 departures in total)

Five weekly A320 (only 10 departures in total)

Two of the routes were to Daytona Beach, which is not overly far from Jacksonville and Orlando. JetBlue has ended all operations there. It first flew to Daytona Beach between January 2016 and January 2019, only to return in December 2025. It was out again after less than a year. Moreover, JetBlue has also entirely pulled out of Manchester, which is not far from Boston, and was only part of its network since January 2025.

They include Orlando to the capital of Costa Rica. This route first welcomed JetBlue in March 2009. Initially, the Embraer E190 was deployed; the type has now been removed from the airline's fleet. Of course, it was nearly all about the A320 (89% of total flights), extremely distantly followed by the A321 (6%) and the E190 (5%).

US Department of Transportation data shows that JetBlue transported approximately 1.5 million round-trip passengers between Orlando and San José between 2009 and 2026. The route's overall load factor in that period was 80.9%. In the final 12 months, the load fell to 77.6%. As usual, this is just one performance measure, and it should not be considered seriously without more data, especially fare information.

They are from five hubs across the US this winter. Find them all here!

The airline did not serve this route, which covers 845 nautical miles (1,565 km) each way, for long. The first flight from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), historically JetBlue's most-served airport, only took off in December 2025.

It was the first time that JFK, which is the Big Apple's busiest airport, had flights to the Florida destination. However, Newark had flights to Vero Beach between January 2016 and February 2023, when the now-defunct Elite Airways operated.

JetBlue ceased JFK-Vero Beach service in September 2026, less than a year after the route began. A 59.5% load factor will do that. So will the route having JetBlue's fifth-lowest length-adjusted total revenue per available seat mile from JFK. It means that Greater NYC is once again unconnected to the city in the Sunshine State.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Booking Holdings took a $900 million revenue reduction and accrued a $100 million loss in the third quarter tied to a potential Federal Trade Commission complaint against its Priceline brand, which the company said is in discussions with the FTC to resolve. In a quarterly filing Tuesday, Booking said the FTC may seek restitution and penalties exceeding $1 billion, plus litigation and similar claims in other jurisdictions, and that litigation remains possible. The company disclosed in the second quarter that the FTC intended to file a complaint against Priceline and a B2B affiliate partner over disclosures, fees, customer support, and billing practices; Reuters reported last month, citing anonymous sources, that the partner is Guest Reservations. The FTC matter runs alongside a European Commission investigation that has called Booking.com's practices for combating fake listings and phishing "substandard." Operationally, net income fell 1% to $2.7 billion on revenue of $8.9 billion, also down 1%, while room nights rose 7%, accelerating from 5% in the second quarter. CFO Ewout Steenbergen described the fourth-quarter travel environment as "mixed," with moderation in international demand and domestic travel holding up as travelers take shorter trips closer to home. Connected trip transactions — bookings across two or more verticals — grew almost 20% year over year and made up a low double-digit share of Booking.com transactions.

#6149. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6148. How everyday families can use the power of credit cards to support their lives

Many of us here at TPG love to leverage our favorite credit cards to enhance our travels. From trying out the newest lie-flat product to relaxing in an airport lounge, these products can go a long way in unlocking memorable experiences.

But for many Americans, credit cards represent a tangible way to support their household's bottom lines — especially in the face of rising costs and the unexpected hurdles that life can throw in their way.

Recently, TPG founder Brian Kelly sat down with three everyday families to help them maximize their wallets — and the conversations demonstrated the true power of making rewards work for you.

Here are some real-world stories that show just what credit cards can unlock for you.

One of the most under-the-radar benefits of credit cards is how they can build financial literacy and set your children up for success in the real world. No, this isn't about giving teens or young adults unfettered access to a big credit limit. Instead, it's the power of adding them as an authorized user to an existing credit card.

That's exactly what we recommended to Seungah Jeong for her 14-year-old daughter, Emi. She just started high school and is starting to spend her own money. By becoming an authorized user on her mom's card, she can start building up a credit history for when she's ready to go off on her own.

Even better? Some cards allow you to set individual spending limits for your authorized users, so your kids can learn about budgeting in a controlled environment.

Everyone has different needs when it comes to credit cards, and making the most of your everyday spending requires two important items. Put simply, you need to know:

If you never eat out, a credit card with a bonus on dining purchases won't do you any good. If you're a frequent international traveler, you don't want to swipe a card and incur foreign transaction fees. And if you focus on earning rewards with a single travel provider, you may be missing out on more flexible rewards.

We saw this play out with all the families we met.

Take the Goralczenkos. Parents Andrew and Tracy have quadruplets who are heading off to college, and both were laid off two years ago when the company they worked for suddenly went out of business. They had been collecting rewards on their favorite theme park credit card for years, but in their current situation, that's not doing much for them.

Instead, they can shift their focus to cash-back rewards, picking up a new card that awards them 3% back on some of their biggest purchases — like gas and groceries.

It was a similar story with Seungah, whose 18-year-old son Oliver was heading off to Greece for college. Our recommendation was to get a new travel rewards card, specifically one that offers flexible rewards and waives foreign transaction fees. That means Oliver won't be hit with up to 3% in fees every time he swipes the card in Europe.

Finally, there was Renee Lewis-Mance. She and her husband, Chris, are retired, but she's very into the points game, focusing primarily on a single airline and a single hotel loyalty program. While these programs can be valuable, Renee is missing out on one of the biggest benefits of being retired: flexibility.

That's why we recommended adding a new transferable rewards card to her wallet. Earning points or miles in one of these programs provides an array of redemption options when she's planning a trip. She's not locked into a single airline or hotel chain, which could limit her options.

Beyond earning with your everyday spending, most popular cards offer one-time bonuses for new applicants (subject to minimum spending requirements). This allows you to take home a big haul of points, miles or cash-back rewards up front while picking up a new card that better fits your spending habits.

This was particularly appealing for the Goralczenkos. The card we recommended came with a $100 welcome bonus, plus 3% back on some major everyday spending categories. That won't get them a flight to Europe, but in their current situation, cash back is much more appealing.

Chris Mance found himself in a similar boat. He was able to grab a one-time, $200 cash-back bonus on a new card that was also a better fit for where he spends his money each month.

But even more importantly, this new card will help him address the final strategy ...

Here at TPG, we like to joke that there's no "point" to using cash for your everyday purchases — but there's certainly risk. Carrying around a bunch of cash leaves you vulnerable to theft, and even if you opt to swipe a debit card, you're generally earning no rewards on those purchases.

That's the exact situation that Chris Mance found himself in. While his wife (Renee) loves playing the points game, Chris usually pays cash or uses a debit card for his regular trips to Home Depot and the grocery store. However, by shifting those purchases to a cash-back credit card, he can unlock some significant rewards.

Based on our estimates, his grocery purchases alone could turn into $250 in cash back every year.

In addition, since Chris was spending a good chunk of money on home improvement purchases — tools, gardening supplies, plants — we recommended a card that will allow him to customize his rewards by picking a category to earn 6% back in the first year. That alone should net him around $300 in rewards.

The best part? This card had no annual fee.

In both cases, Chris isn't spending more money than he already planned to spend. He's just switching to a payment method that rewards him for his existing spending habits.

The world of credit cards features an array of products to meet the needs of virtually every American. Sure, there are options geared toward luxury travelers with a variety of benefits to help elevate their next trip. But many others can be a great fit for everyday pursuits, like shopping at the grocery store or building your child's credit history.

Ordinary families can easily take advantage of cash-back rewards to support their household bottom lines, and can boost their earnings by carefully analyzing their spending habits to select the best card(s) for their wallets.

And as long as you're responsibly managing your credit and spending within your means, the only way to lose is by not participating at all.

#6146. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

This is some good news, and I see the XP rates are restored now. I have two flights early Jan that I planned to buy XP for. But I usually wait until closer to departure dates in case I need to change plans. I'll jump in and get those purchased now!

For US Residents: Not for anything, but my understanding is that the Bank of America Flying Blue credit card is eminently churnable. I have a friend who got the card in 2022, cancelled it, got it again in 2023, cancelled it, and got it again this year. This may be an easy way to get 100 XPs when/if needed, though with all things points and credit, YMMV; this is just a data point.

Would've been better to roll it out like this originally.

Can I lock in the 10 eur/xp rate if I pay now for a flight in January?

The secrets are always the same - give some advance notice, over-communicate, don't be patronizing ("our customers asked for this...") and just tell it like it is. Flying Blue didn't do that, and now they did. Kudos to Tiffany for rectifying a small mistake, but a mistake nonetheless.

#6145. How Much Premium Economy Costs On London-New York Flights In 2026

Premium economy on a London-New York flight can cost more than twice as much as an economy ticket, but the difference between the two cabins and business class can sometimes be surprisingly small. For passengers facing an approximately eight-hour transatlantic journey, a wider seat, extra legroom, better meals, and extra baggage can be appealing, but does the experience justify the added cost?

In 2026, passengers traveling between London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and New York JFK Airport have several airlines to choose from, including British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and JetBlue. Those flying to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) have fewer nonstop options, primarily British Airways and United Airlines. With different premium economy products, competing fares, and varying baggage allowances, how much should passengers actually expect to pay for a more comfortable transatlantic journey?

Premium economy on the London-New York route typically costs approximately $1,000 to $1,300 for a return journey, compared with around $500 to $600 for a standard economy ticket. This means passengers can expect to pay roughly twice as much for the upgraded cabin, although the difference depends on the airline, travel dates, departure airport, and availability.

According to our analysis of premium economy fares in 2026, the transatlantic market demonstrates how airlines position their intermediate cabin between standard economy and business class. Premium economy has become a major revenue opportunity for carriers, letting them charge more for added comfort without offering the considerably more expensive lie-flat seating associated with business class.

However, the difference between cabins isn't always consistent. A NerdWallet comparison of British Airways fares found that one evening departure from New York JFK to London offered premium economy for $1,162, more than twice the $532 economy fare. Business class was available for just $1,222, meaning passengers would have saved only $60 by selecting premium economy instead. Another comparison showed a return premium economy fare of $1,459 against $737 in economy. These examples raise an important question: how much competition exists between airlines on the route, and where can passengers find the best selection?

The greatest selection of nonstop services is available between London Heathrow and New York JFK. According to FlightConnections, five airlines serve the route: British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and JetBlue. The route covers approximately 3,440 miles (5,536 kilometers), with flights generally taking around eight hours.

However, passengers should distinguish between the airlines operating the route and those offering a dedicated premium economy cabin. British Airways calls its intermediate product World Traveller Plus, Virgin Atlantic markets its cabin as Premium, and American Airlines offers Premium Economy on eligible long-haul aircraft. Delta also operates Premium Select on eligible international services. JetBlue, meanwhile, offers its Mint business class and Even More Space economy seating rather than a conventional dedicated premium economy cabin.

The situation is different for passengers traveling to Newark. According to FlightConnections' LHR-EWR route information, British Airways and United Airlines operate nonstop flights between the two airports: United's intermediate product corresponding to British Airways’ World Traveller Plus is called Premium Plus. The route covers approximately 3,454 miles (5,559 km), with an average flight time of seven hours and 55 minutes.

British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American, Delta, JetBlue

World Traveller Plus, Premium, Premium Economy, Premium Select

Such a variety of airlines at JFK makes it attractive to travelers seeking schedule flexibility and competitive fares. Nevertheless, more airline options do not automatically mean cheaper premium economy tickets. British Airways and Virgin Atlantic offer useful examples of what passengers can expect to pay.

A closer look at the price bump that is required to fly in BA's Club cabins.

British Airways and Virgin Atlantic are two of the most prominent competitors on the London-New York market, and both offer dedicated premium economy cabins on their long-haul services. Their current fares demonstrate that passengers departing London can sometimes find considerably more attractive prices than those booking an equivalent journey from the United States.

Virgin Atlantic's official website provides a particularly useful snapshot of its pricing. For a return journey from London Heathrow to New York JFK between November 17 and November 22, 2026, the airline advertised Premium fares starting at approximately $1,529. Its published offers for selected dates in May, July, and August 2027 also showed starting fares of approximately $1,542 to $1,549. These are advertised starting prices, not guaranteed fares for every departure.

The airline's official Premium flight deals page also provides information about its cabin and included services. British Airways, meanwhile, allows passengers to compare World Traveller Plus fares through its official website.

Furthermore, the KAYAK sample for February 5–12, 2027 provides another useful comparison point during low season, with prices slightly lower than those for immediate departures within two weeks, although those dates fall outside the 2026 calendar year. With the fares set, the next question is what passengers get for spending more than £1,000 on a return ticket.

One of the main advantages of premium economy is extra personal space, which can make a big difference on an overnight transatlantic journey or for passengers with health issues. British Airways' World Traveller Plus cabin features wider seats, additional legroom, greater recline, lumbar support, and adjustable headrests and footrests. Passengers also receive an enhanced meal service, complimentary bar service, personal entertainment systems, and priority boarding.

Virgin Atlantic's Premium cabin offers a similarly upgraded experience, although the precise seat specifications depend on the aircraft operating the flight. According to its official cabin information, the airline offers up to 38 inches of seat pitch, additional room to stretch out, and a footrest. Its onboard experience also includes restaurant-inspired meals served on porcelain dishware, a welcome glass of bubbly, and additional snacks on selected aircraft.

Baggage is another important consideration when calculating the actual cost difference between economy and premium economy. Virgin Atlantic Premium includes two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds (23 kg) each, plus a 22-pound (10-kg) hand luggage allowance. British Airways World Traveller Plus also provides two checked bags on most routes, while some economy fares are hand-baggage-only tickets. According to NerdWallet, adding two checked bags to certain British Airways economy bookings can cost up to $175 each way.

These additional services make premium economy more than simply an upgraded seat. However, the cabin doesn't offer the same experience as business class, especially for sleeping arrangements and airport lounge access. This distinction becomes important when the price difference between the two cabins starts to narrow.

The price difference between premium economy and business class fares is not always huge. Airlines use dynamic pricing systems that adjust ticket prices according to demand, remaining inventory, booking patterns, and the number of seats available in each fare category. As a result, a premium economy ticket can occasionally approach the price of a discounted business class seat, especially when demand for the intermediate cabin is high.

NerdWallet’s British Airways example illustrates this well. One New York JFK departure offered premium economy for $1,162, compared with $532 for economy and $1,222 for business class. In this comparison, choosing premium economy instead of business class saved only $60. For passengers seeking the additional comfort of a fully flat bed on an overnight flight, that relatively small difference could make business class a more attractive option.

Passengers also have another option when considering British Airways: using Avios. According to Award Travel Finder's London-New York redemption analysis, a one-way off-peak World Traveller Plus redemption requires 46,750 Avios, increasing to 66,000 during peak periods. Economy requires 27,500 Avios off-peak and 33,000 during peak periods. Taxes and charges are additional, meaning passengers must compare the monetary cost of an award ticket with the cash fare before deciding whether redemption represents good value.

Available loyalty points and occasional business-class promotions make comparing all three cabins especially important. Nevertheless, for passengers without enough points or who can't find attractive business class fares, premium economy remains an interesting middle ground. The question is whether the added comfort justifies the higher cost on this transatlantic route.

Premium economy occupies an interesting niche in the London-New York market because it provides a noticeable improvement over standard economy, often without the substantial expense of business class. On an approximately eight-hour journey, additional legroom, wider seats, improved dining, and priority airport services can make a meaningful difference for some passengers.

However, the financial case weakens when the fare approaches business-class pricing. A passenger paying $1,162 for premium economy when business class costs $1,222 is arguably better off considering the higher cabin, provided the business class fare is genuinely available for the same itinerary and booking conditions. Conversely, Virgin Atlantic's advertised return fare of $1,529 for November 2026 demonstrates that premium economy can be considerably more accessible than some of the higher-priced examples found in the US market.

Competition also gives passengers some flexibility. Travelers to JFK can compare British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, American Airlines, Delta, and JetBlue, while Newark offers British Airways and United as nonstop options. Checking both New York airports, comparing departure dates, and examining the differences between economy, premium economy, and business class can reveal opportunities that aren't immediately apparent when searching for a single airline.

Premium economy isn't automatically worth twice the price of economy, but the cheapest available ticket isn't necessarily the best option. The deciding factor will be the actual fare difference on the selected dates, the baggage and onboard benefits included, and how much passengers value additional comfort during their transatlantic journey.
