#6126. Hotel CEOs Reveal Where They Think Travel Is Headed—But AI Could Make Them Lower Room Prices

GHA Discovery asked hotel CEOs what will shape their business over the next few years, and 87% expect AI assistants to be among the most important booking channels by 2030. They expect hotel websites and loyalty programs to matter more than online travel agencies. Hotels would love to stop paying commissions to Expedia and Booking.com. But I think they’re overlooking how much harder a sufficiently capable AI will make it to charge customers more than they need to pay. Hotels may get more direct bookings while earning less from each guest booking direct. The short GHA Hotel Brand CEO Outlook 2027 is worth reading. GHA Discovery connects about 60 brands and 1,000 hotels, including Kempinski, Anantara, Capella, Pan Pacific, NH and smaller groups like Lore. I think the program gets far less attention than it deserves and I’ve had some fantastic stays. What Hotel CEOs Expect This was an August survey of 30 CEOs from GHA brands: They’re worried, but still expect growth. 90% named geopolitical instability among their biggest challenges over the next five years. Nearly half expect like-for-like hotel revenue to grow at least 5% in 2027. (Notably, GHA itself is based in Dubai.) International leisure travel is the growth engine. 73% expect international demand to outperform domestic, and 90% expect international leisure travel to increase. India is almost as widely cited as the United States. 53% named the U.S. as a source of international growth, versus 50% for India and 40% each for China and the U.K. AI is expected to dominate hotel discovery. For influence on bookings in 2030, AI assistants scored 87%, hotel websites and apps 50%, loyalty platforms 47%, and online travel agencies 30%. Loyalty matters, and recognition leads their list of differentiators. 83% consider loyalty critical or very important to revenue growth. Recognition was selected by 70% as a factor distinguishing successful programs, versus 57% for personalization and 47% for rewards. India is significant, a small share of a very large population crossing the income threshold for international travel produces a lot of customers. India had 32.83 million departures by Indian nationals in 2025, up 6.3%. And the number of people there worth more than $30 million grew 63% between 2021 and 2026. The opportunity comes from the number of people who can afford to travel, rather than population numbers themselves. The finding in the report I’m skeptical of is only 13% selecting price as a leading influence on hotel decisions in 2030. Unless money just no longer matters in a post-AGI world (!) this seems implausible. Hotel brand also scored just 13%, compared with 43% for loyalty benefits. An AI recommendation can be based on price. Putting “AI recommendations” and “price” in separate buckets doesn’t establish that price stops mattering to the AI. Hotels Can Lose Pricing Power Even As More Guests Book Direct Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value. They bring customers. Someone may not know the hotel exists, may not have a preferred chain, or may want to compare properties across chains. Expedia, Booking.com and others supply an audience the hotel doesn’t reach on its own. They help hotels charge different customers different prices. A hotel wants to sell rooms that would otherwise sit empty without cutting the price for everyone who would’ve paid more. Packages, restricted membership rates and opaque offers can let them discount without putting the same lower rate on their own site. I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option. The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings. If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating. This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout. An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room. It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it. I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. They may avoid OTA commissions but get rates competed down, and while lower commissions apply only to a limited piece of their business, the lower rates would affect the entire hotel. An unknown hotel may gain enough customers to come out well ahead. A unique property on a sold out night has pricing power. But more direct bookings may or may not mean greater profits. Recognition Doesn’t Replace Rewards The report’s loyalty finding interests me because I’ve been writing about recognition and reward as the twin pillars of loyalty for more than a decade. They’re different things, and a good program does both. Recognition can be the thing a traveler values most. But if getting it means giving up the rebate they’d earn elsewhere, they’re actually having to pay for that recognition. A guest may care more about their treatment but that’s holding rewards constant. GHA addressed this when it relaunched Discovery in December 2021. Previously, it offered status benefits and Local Experience awards. Those awards could be great, but a business traveler working all day often had no use for the experience on offer. Discovery Dollars gave members a flexible rebate they could put toward a hotel bill. The CEO survey asks what will differentiate successful programs. That’s compatible with rewards being something customers already expect. It doesn’t mean you can take the rewards away. And in GHA’s separate research among more than 9,000 members this year, generosity was the leading program attribute. Ease of earning and spending Discovery Dollars and hotel benefits both rated highly. Why I Value GHA Discovery I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. Hyatt still has the advantages of confirmed suites at booking, guaranteed late checkout at most properties and a more consistent breakfast benefit. GHA gives me interesting hotels where I still receive real benefits. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I wound up in the suite that used to be the bank’s boardroom, with a dining table for 12. I’d booked through Chase’s The Edit and stacked its benefits with GHA status. At Kempinski Cancun, I combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA and received an oceanfront suite and club access. Members earn 4% to 7% back in Discovery Dollars on eligible spending, depending on status. One Discovery Dollar is worth one U.S. dollar toward eligible spending at participating hotels. Titanium earns 7%, with those regularly earned dollars valid for 24 months. Promotional dollars can expire sooner. Titanium includes a two-category upgrade, 11 a.m. early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability. Breakfast for two is included at participating brands on direct bookings. You can earn Titanium with 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The last route can mean just three one-night stays (NH Hotels, NH Collection and nhow count together as one brand). At the Lyle in D.C., the staff arranged fresh coffee for me at 5 a.m., two hours before room service opened. It arrived at exactly 5 a.m. That’s the sort of thing I remember and go back for. I’ve also covered their unusually accessible status matches. The current offer runs through November 30, 2026, with approved status lasting through December 31, 2027: Platinum: $100 application fee, with D$50 back. Titanium: $150 application fee, with D$75 back. There’s no stay challenge. Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above are among the statuses that match to Titanium. Eligible airline and cruise status, and some credit cards, qualify too. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and the terms allow only one GHA status match. For someone with an upcoming stay at one of these hotels, $150 with $75 back in hotel spending can be a very good way to get treated better. I’d like my future travel assistant to notice that before it tells me I’ve saved $20 booking the same hotel without benefits through Expedia. Online travel agencies do two things that hotels value.

I’ve written about how hotels distribute discounted inventory outside their public rates, and why a card travel portal can sometimes beat the hotel’s own member price. Booking direct isn’t automatically the cheapest option.

The hotel has room to be more generous when it isn’t spending on the OTA commission. It can give some of that money to the guest as a lower price, rewards or benefits. The agency has its own operating costs and profit to cover. It seems like a chain could undercut the third party. But today’s room rate isn’t fixed while AI just redistributes the savings.

If AI can find the right small hotel even though I’ve never heard of it, that’s less reason to start with Expedia and more reason to book direct. But it’s also less reason to pay a premium for the familiar hotel I would’ve booked without doing much research. And where there are opaque offers the AI may find those too. It could ask several suitable hotels for their best offer, comparing cash discounts with credits and benefits, and without my needing to spend time negotiating.

This already matters in my own choices. In Venice, I wanted a location that worked for my family, rather than staying on Murano just to use Hyatt. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi, GHA status helped me with early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout.

An assistant that knows my family’s needs can compare that entire package against the alternatives. It can consider a different neighborhood, a different destination, or different dates, rather than just finding another website selling the same room.

It can also work through offers that are currently tedious to find. Opaque hotels become less opaque if the assistant can identify them from their amenities, location and photos. Still, knowing about a corporate rate doesn’t make you eligible for it.

I’d expect pressure on direct booking margins because consumers have the intelligence in their pockets that just solved math. I was not quite sure what this article was about. Is it about GHA? You were right in a previous post, I know little about it. Maybe I should find out.

If it is about booking directly, Nike’s attempt to force everyone to buy their shoes directly was a disaster. Booking engines provide visibility, even to major brands. I still use Agoda to book in Asia, even though it is now owned by Booking Holdings. For small hotels, like a nice family hotel with dinky clean rooms I stayed in Tokyo or the great one bedroom suite with a free breakfast in Phnom Penh, Agoda opens up a world market.

If it about AI, AI might help. However, (1) My iphone AI news app has decided that I want to read food and recipe, celerity, puzzles. I cannot figure out how to turn off the feed of crap stories. (2) My Youtube app has decided to push a steady stream of AI generated content, that mostly is taken from Wikipedia and shorts. I cannot seem to turn it off, so I turned off all suggestions and search. (3) My Netflicks app has decided I like Korean movies (I have no idea why), and sends me pages of suggestions. I cannot get it to stop. It gives me a headache, and I don’t watch anything. I might cancel Netflicks (4) Don’t get me started about customer service AI. Until I see AI working in my own life, I am naturally skeptical that AI will solve my hotel choices any time soon.

The main problem is incentives. Hotel operators actual customers are not guests; it’s property owners. Rarely do these corporations own the underlying real estate. So, they don’t really care about consumers so much as shareholders, property owners, and their own executive compensation. Fix the incentives; magically, consumers will be treated better. At the very least, better guardrails to protect from outright fraud, deceptive practices, please.

Yeah, just charge a resort fee and for parking in the middle of Nebraska hotels.

#6124. The Unproven Economics of the Weekend Cruise

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto shorter trips. Grok

Cruise lines are putting some of their biggest ships on shorter trips, but the financial evidence that those voyages generate better returns remains thin.

Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto three- and four-night trips, betting that shorter vacations will bring customers back more often. But more passengers are not the same as more profit. Norwegian shortened its average cruise this year, carried 24% more guests, and earned less revenue and gross margin per passenger-day. That does not prove short cruises are bad business, but it does mean the weekend math needs more scrutiny.

For decades, the industry sold seven-night vacations. As ships grew larger and added water parks, more restaurants, and bigger shows, short sailings went to older, smaller ships that sold for less.

Disney was already doing this with the Wish in 2022, and Virgin Voyages launched its first ship on four- and five-night Caribbean itineraries in 2021.

Royal Caribbean took the strategy to megaship scale in 2024 when it put Utopia of the Seas, a new Oasis-class ship, straight into t

Cruise lines are putting their newest and largest ships on three- and four-night itineraries, a break from the seven-night template the industry built its economics around. Royal Caribbean started it at megaship scale with Utopia of the Seas from Port Canaveral in 2024, and Carnival will follow with Mardi Gras on four- and five-day Bahamas sailings from the same port in May 2027. The logic is frequency: a ship running alternating short trips serves two sets of guests a week instead of one, doubling embarkations and the chance to sell drink packages, specialty dining, and excursions. Royal Caribbean Group CEO Jason Liberty said on the October 27 earnings call that half of the group's guests are millennials or younger, that they spend about as much on a short trip as on a seven-night cruise, and that onboard spending has beaten expectations. The filings are harder to read. Royal Caribbean's revenue per passenger-day rose only to about $320 from $315 in the first nine months of 2026, with ticket revenue per passenger-day flat, and its average voyage barely shortened, from 6.2 days to 6.1. Norwegian, which has cut its average cruise from about 8.6 days to 7.5, carried 24% more passengers but saw revenue per passenger-day fall from $401 to $385 and gross margin per passenger-day drop nearly 11%. Neither company reports results by cruise length, so the weekend model's profitability cannot be verified from public disclosures.

#6123. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

#6122. Senator Chris Murphy “awake and alert” after suffering a stroke

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized after suffering a stroke Saturday afternoon while attending his son’s hockey game, his office announced Sunday.

The 53-year-old senator began experiencing numbness in his arm and was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he had suffered a stroke. He was subsequently transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for further monitoring.

“He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment,” Murphy’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement.

Chris Murphy’s chief says the 53-year-old Democratic senator had a stroke.

“Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”

“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” she added.

Murphy is actually the fourth Senate Democrat to suffer a stroke in recent years. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland both suffered strokes in 2022 and subsequently recovered. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania also suffered a stroke that year while campaigning for office and now uses live-captioning technology to assist with auditory processing during Senate proceedings.

Murphy, who has represented Connecticut in the Senate since 2013, has emerged as a prominent Democratic voice on gun control and immigration. He is also considered a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The senator has spent recent weeks campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. He was scheduled to appear Sunday in New Hampshire alongside Democratic candidates Chris Pappas and Stefany Shaheen. Murphy is not on Tuesday’s ballot.

Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont, who campaigned alongside Murphy on Friday, said he and his wife were keeping the senator and his family in their prayers.

Lawmakers from both parties also expressed support, including Sens. John Fetterman, D-Pa., and Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa.

Murphy’s office has not announced a timeline for his release from the hospital.

#6121. Air Serbia Flight Turns Back As Spy Onboard Accused Of Bypassing Security

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and flying back to Belgrade, where everyone had to get off and go through security again. Reportedly Serbia’s former intelligence chief was allowed to board without completing security screening. He says he’s being targeted by political opponents. The flight eventually reached Moscow about seven hours late, with spy master Aleksandar Vulin still onboard. Flight JU134 departed Belgrade at 6:48 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3. The Airbus A320, registration YU-APH, turned back over southern Lithuania and landed back in Belgrade at 9:56 p.m. That’s more than three hours of flying to end up where passengers started. Flightradar24 tracks Air Serbia flight JU134 returning to Belgrade after turning around over Lithuania. Also onboard were Dušan Bajatović, who runs state gas company Srbijagas, and politician Nenad Popović. Bajatović. Everyone and their luggage went through another inspection. Passengers reboarded shortly before 2 a.m., and a replacement crew took over because of duty time limits. According to Belgrade’s Third Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office: Police contacted the duty prosecutor at 8:26 p.m. They described a passenger passing through the security area with an officer from Serbia’s intelligence agency without the required screening. A police memo received the next day added that the passenger had triggered an alarm and hadn’t received the additional inspection. Radio audio circulated by Serbian media includes the captain telling passengers the return was for security reasons, along with instructions to the crew after landing. Radio communication from the return of Air Serbia flight JU134, shared by journalist Žarko Bogosavljević. Vulin denies wrongdoing. He says he slept through the flight, woke up back in Belgrade, and found police waiting. His account includes asking them, “Colleagues, have you come for me?” He says they laughed and told him they hadn’t. He says he passed the checks, nothing illegal was found, and the whole thing was an attempt to impress the country’s incoming political leadership. His stated reason for going to Moscow was to seek an extension of Serbia’s gas agreement with Russia. He subsequently posted from Moscow denying that he’d fled Serbia. Aleksandar Vulin’s response after arriving in Moscow. Vulin has been Serbia’s defense minister, interior minister, intelligence chief and deputy prime minister. The United States sanctioned him in 2023, alleging corruption and assistance to Russian influence operations. His political ally Aleksandar Vučić’s side lost Serbia’s October 25 election. I’ve covered an American Airlines Charlotte–Cancun flight that returned after a former airline employee bypassed screening, so returning a flight over an unscreened passenger isn’t unique to Serbia. Here, though, the aircraft was much farther along. Returning to the airport that identified the problem puts the passenger, the screeners and the surveillance records under the same authorities. And it may be difficult (and embarrassing) to coordinate with a closer airport in another country to handle this and without the airline’s same presence on the ground. Belgrade’s prosecutor’s office is now seeking answers from the airport’s security director, including who ordered the return, what security assessment supported it, whether procedures were violated before departure, and who authorized the flight to leave again. Vulin denies wrongdoing. He says he slept through the flight, woke up back in Belgrade, and found police waiting. His account includes asking them, “Colleagues, have you come for me?” He says they laughed and told him they hadn’t.

He says he passed the checks, nothing illegal was found, and the whole thing was an attempt to impress the country’s incoming political leadership. His stated reason for going to Moscow was to seek an extension of Serbia’s gas agreement with Russia. He subsequently posted from Moscow denying that he’d fled Serbia.

Aleksandar Vulin’s response after arriving in Moscow.

Vulin has been Serbia’s defense minister, interior minister, intelligence chief and deputy prime minister. The United States sanctioned him in 2023, alleging corruption and assistance to Russian influence operations. His political ally Aleksandar Vučić’s side lost Serbia’s October 25 election.

I’ve covered an American Airlines Charlotte–Cancun flight that returned after a former airline employee bypassed screening, so returning a flight over an unscreened passenger isn’t unique to Serbia. Here, though, the aircraft was much farther along.

Returning to the airport that identified the problem puts the passenger, the screeners and the surveillance records under the same authorities. And it may be difficult (and embarrassing) to coordinate with a closer airport in another country to handle this and without the airline’s same presence on the ground.

Belgrade’s prosecutor’s office is now seeking answers from the airport’s security director, including who ordered the return, what security assessment supported it, whether procedures were violated before departure, and who authorized the flight to leave again.

Earn 2 Delta Comfort Flight Certificates + 50K Miles

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

For small-business owners who love to fly with American Airlines, the (see rates and fees) should be in your crosshairs.

It's an affordable card with no annual fee for the first cardholder year (then a $99 annual fee; this fee increases to a $150 annual fee for renewals after Jan. 24, 2027). That gives you a chance to try out its free checked bags, preferred boarding and bonus miles on several common business expenses without committing to a fee for the first year.

But because it overlaps heavily with the airline perks on personal American Airlines cards, it makes the most sense for side hustlers and small businesses that don’t already carry a similar credit card or those looking to add to their mileage balance through business spending. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The offers a moderate set of benefits without the treasure trove of partner offers, elite status boosts and lounge perks found on more premium cards.

This card's benefits favor travelers who prefer to fly with American Airlines, but it doesn't require a full commitment to the airline thanks to its manageable annual fee (after the first cardholder year).

Cardholders will receive the following American Airlines-centric perks:

In addition to the benefits just mentioned, cardholders have access to these perks:

The is a mid-tier airline card with standout perks like free checked bags, no-additional-fee employee cards and Loyalty Points on spending.

Given that checking bags with American costs at least $45 per bag one-way, you can practically recoup this card's annual fee after the first cardholder year by checking a bag on three one-way flights. If you travel with an employee or another companion, it becomes easy to extract even more value — assuming you would otherwise pay for checked bags.

You'll need to spend $30,000 in a cardholder year to earn a companion certificate ($99 plus taxes and fees). That's an incredibly high spending requirement for a mid-tier card that earns just 1 mile per dollar on nonbonus purchases.

The card includes basic business management resources, but its benefits still lean heavily toward American Airlines travel rather than premium business tools.

You won’t get statement credits for business partners or other features offered by more robust business cards. From a perks standpoint, the Citi / AAdvantage Business is extremely similar to the personal , though the earning rates are better suited to business spending.

The earns miles in a relatively broad selection of categories. Cardholders earn:

Starting Jan. 24, 2027, the card is undergoing a refresh that will add two new bonus-earning categories.

There aren't many cards that offer bonus earnings on telecommunication services, so the AAdvantage Business is a viable option for those expenses. Cardholders could also get a lot of value out of the choice category once it launches in 2027. You'll be able to select your preferred earnings category and can change it once a quarter, if you prefer. All the options overlap nicely with common business purchases.

Ironically, this card may not be the best option for American Airlines airfare. Some cards outearn it, such as the .

Remember that you'll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent on all purchases, helping you get closer to elite status with American.

When it's time to redeem the miles you earn, your best bet is to book award flights. In addition to flights operated by American Airlines, you can use your miles on partner airlines such as Alaska Airlines or Finnair.

TPG credit cards writer Becky Pokora recently redeemed 55,000 miles for a one-way trip from Johannesburg (JNB) to Berlin (BER) in business class on Oneworld partner Qatar Airways for travel in 2027. That’s more than 14 hours in a premium cabin for fewer miles than you can earn through the card’s introductory offer.

You can also use your AAdvantage miles for flight upgrades, hotels, car rentals, vacation packages, cruises and Admirals Club passes. Aside from cabin upgrades on flights, these options generally provide less value than award flights.

Related: Why American Airlines AAdvantage has become my most valuable rewards currency

The Citi / AAdvantage Business will become more useful after its 2027 refresh, but its annual fee is rising from $99 to $150. That makes it harder to justify if you don’t use the new inflight or Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credits.

Most purchases will still earn just 1 mile per dollar, and only one of the three selectable business categories can earn 2 miles per dollar at a time.

Related: Which AAdvantage card is right for you? Here are 3 options you should consider

The AAdvantage Business and Platinum Select share most of their airline perks, so the decision comes down to whether you need a business account, which bonus categories fit your spending and whether you value the Business card’s companion certificate or the Platinum Select’s new lifestyle perks.

The Platinum Select, though, has stronger rewards on restaurant spending and will add bonus spending categories for select streaming services, electric vehicle charging and eligible rides and rails purchases beginning Jan. 24, 2027.

You'll still get free checked bags, preferred boarding, Loyalty Points on card spending and inflight savings with the Platinum Select.

Choose the Citi / AAdvantage Business if you want to separate your business expenses, add employee cards and earn bonus miles on more business-specific purchases, like telecommunications, U.S. advertising, U.S. shipping or office supplies.

The Platinum Select is the better fit if you don’t need a business account. Because their core American Airlines benefits overlap, most travelers won’t need both.

The Citi / AAdvantage Business is worth it for small-business owners who fly American often enough to use the airline benefits. The addition of statement credits toward eligible inflight purchases could provide more value to offset the annual fee, even though that cost is going up in 2027.

At $150 after the first year, it will be less compelling for cardholders who already receive similar American Airlines perks from another card or via elite status. It’s also not ideal as an everyday spending card, since most purchases earn just 1 mile per dollar spent.

For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. This offer is the highest we've seen in the card’s recent public offers, making it an excellent time to apply.

According to TPG's November 2026 valuations, these bonus miles are worth $1,088.

Before submitting your application, make sure to consider Citi's application rules.

I've already mentioned the Platinum Select as a strong competitor, but here are some other options to think about:

For additional options, check out our picks for the best American Airlines cards and the best travel rewards cards.

The upcoming refresh will make the Citi / AAdvantage Business more versatile—but also more expensive. Its new business bonus category and statement credits can justify the upcharge for frequent American flyers who will use them naturally. The free checked bag benefit can also offset the annual fee, especially when employees or companions travel on the same reservation.

If you already have an AAdvantage card, you might not find the AAdvantage Business as compelling. But if this is your first foray into American Airlines' cards, it's worth giving the AAdvantage Business a shot.

#6119. Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways Sale: Save Up To 50% On Award Flights

Alaska Atmos Rewards offers the Global Getaways promotion, whereby members can save on award tickets in select regions. Atmos Rewards launches this promotion on the first Wednesday of each month (which the program calls “Atmos Members Day”), so we just saw the one for November launched.

Let’s go over the opportunities, as you can save up to 50% on award tickets. There are some cool markets in which you can save miles, though unfortunately only economy travel qualifies.

For the new Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways promotion, you can save up to 50% on award travel to nine destinations, with the following restrictions:

The theme for this Global Getaways promotion is “lights, camera, departure,” with the idea being to “roll out the red carpet for the destinations that have starred in your favorite films and shows.” With this sale, you can save on one-way redemptions to the following destinations (these savings are up to 50%, but not always that high):

I very much appreciate Alaska Atmos Rewards’ creativity with this promotion, as nowadays it’s pretty rare to see programs offer award sales that are also valid for travel on partner airlines. Now, admittedly I wish there weren’t quite as many restrictions in terms of the booking window, travel period, the class of service limitations, and the one-way discount, but still, there will be value here for some, and it’s better than nothing.

If you’re simply looking for the lowest cost award, some of these award prices are very tough to beat. For example, getting from the mainland to Hawaii for 11,500 points is a great deal, as is getting from the United States to India for 30,000 points. Keep in mind that with Atmos Rewards, award flights even earn status points, so could help you qualify for status.

I do hope that over time we see some first and business class award sales as well (it’s probably not happening, but we can dream, right?). Many of us have historically loved the program for the value it offers for premium cabin travel, so this promotion doesn’t help us much with that.

This is basically Alaska’s version of Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards or Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes, except it applies for travel on partner airlines (rather than just for travel on the program’s airline), and is exclusive to economy (while the other promotions are mixed).

Alaska Atmos Rewards has launched its latest Global Getaways promotion, which is a monthly redemption deal offering up to a 50% discount on awards. This time around, you can save points on economy redemptions to select destinations. You need to book by November 7, 2026, mostly for travel in early 2027. While this won’t be useful for everyone, I imagine some people will get value from this.

What do you make of Alaska’s Global Getaways promotion?

#6118. The dark paradox of Israel’s election — and ours

Benjamin Netanyahu didnât win last weekâs election in Israel. But he didnât exactly lose it either. The real loser may have been Israelâs fragile democracy, already corrupted from within, perhaps past the point of no return, by Netanyahuâs decades-long death-grip on power.

On the eve of a momentous election in the United States, the parallels are both inexact and unavoidable. Israelis must now decide what kind of country they will have, or at least what kind they aspire to have. They must decide whose votes actually count, and whether some citizens are more equal than others.Â

Those same questions also confront Americans, both in this weekâs midterm elections and, in a more general sense, on the larger political and historical stage. No doubt it is tempting for liberals and progressives to express outrage at the blatant flaws and contradictions of Israeli democracy. But to invoke the Christian tradition here, it might be better to remove the plank from your own eye before trying to remove the speck from your brotherâs.Â

On the surface, the electoral arithmetic in Israel appears straightforward. Parties opposed to Netanyahuâs far-right government won 67 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israelâs parliament. So a majority coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces is clearly achievable, right? You would think so, except that 19 of those 67 seats were won by Israelâs âArab parties,â an all-time high, and that startling fact has thrown the entire political system into confusion.

Netanyahu and his allies have spent the last week airing groundless allegations that the election was fraudulent or rigged, a refrain that Americans are likely to hear a great deal in coming days. What the Zionist far right means is that too many Israeli Arabs â meaning the Palestinian population that remained in Israel after the state was created in 1948 â decided to vote this time, an outcome that no one expected, and that none of the parties representing the Jewish majority particularly wanted.Â

Now, in a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.Â

In a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who leads the centrist-Zionist opposition to Netanyahu, promised during the campaign not to form a government with Arab support. Over the last several nights, thousands of demonstrators in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem have urged him to do precisely that, since the only realistic alternative is the grim default setting of Israeli politics: another wobbly right-wing government headed by Netanyahu, which means more brutality and destruction in Gaza, more war with Iran and more settler violence in the West Bank.Â

As Gideon Levy of the left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz explains it,Â

The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that?

The electionâs unexpected results are âa cause for rejoicing,â Levy writes, in that they have presented Israelis with a clear choice âbetween a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties.â If the âchange blocâ within the Zionist majority cannot accept a coalition with Arab Israelis, he continues, âthey will make it clear that they are actually the same as Netanyahu, that they prefer even the devil Netanyahu over repressing their racism. â¦ [E]veryone will know that racism is the supreme value in this country, across the board, above any other value.â

That ferocious language certainly does not represent mainstream Israeli opinion, but itâs fair to say the strong emotion beneath Levyâs words is far more widely felt. I donât think itâs possible for a non-Jewish observer (such as myself), however well educated or sympathetic, to understand the anguish felt by Jewish people â wherever they live, and whatever their political views â at the enormous distance between what Israel originally represented to the world, or claimed to represent, and what it represents now.

Iâm old enough to remember when most American liberals and progressives viewed the state of Israel in overwhelmingly positive terms, as a locus of charismatic or heroic renewal for the people Hitler couldnât kill, infused with the spirit of European socialism and, not far below the surface, the collective guilt of the Holocaust. I grew up in one of the most left-liberal corners of America, surrounded by educated adults who supported the civil rights movement, opposed the Vietnam War, hated Richard Nixon and loved Israel. Golda Meir and Moshe Dayan were beloved celebrities; the Six-Day War of 1967 and the Yom Kippur War of 1973, as narrated by U.S. media, were straight-up battles between the forces of light and darkness.Â

That says more about the moral blindness or willful innocence of American liberalism, I must admit, than it says about Israel. In any event, when I saw Joe Bidenâs fateful bear hug with Netanyahu on the tarmac of Ben Gurion Airport in the aftermath of the dreadful Oct. 7 attack, I understood it. I recognized the country Biden was coming from, because I came from there too: It was the Democratic majority of the not-so-distant past, when Israel was embraced as a light to the nations and left-wing radicals who brought up the Palestinian cause were being unreasonable hotheads, if not openly antisemitic and a little bit Nazi.Â

What Israel has become during Netanyahuâs long and destructive reign is now clear to most of the world, and most of all to the many Jewish or Israeli critics who have been speaking difficult truths for many years, often at enormous personal cost. I am disinclined, however, to judge too harshly those who cling to the vision of Israel as an exceptional nation â one that has stumbled, perhaps, but may yet regain its true path.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Like I said earlier, we should mind the plank in our own eye first. Isnât that the same vision that many Americans still cling to? That somehow, on the other side of this dreadful phase of our history â yes, a full decade of Donald Trump, but Iâm afraid the damage goes back a lot further than that â the âindispensable nationâ variously articulated by Abraham Lincoln, John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama is still there, still retrievable, still bending its moral arc toward justice.

Americans and Israelis are conjoined by history, for better or worse, and now see each other as distorted reflections, through a glass darkly, as the King James Bible puts it. We face versions of the same decisions this week, about whose votes count and whether the highfalutin words of our constitution apply to everyone. About whether to see terror and tyranny for what they are, and turn the page.

from Andrew OâHehir on our bewildering world

Choice Hotels paid Barcelona-based Sercotel $24.3 million in September to exit an acquisition agreement, a person familiar with the transaction told Skift. Choice disclosed the payout in its latest quarterly filing without naming the company, noting it terminated the buy-out agreement on September 16. On the earnings call, CEO Dominic Dragisich said what began as an option to buy full ownership "eventually migrated to an obligation," and that Choice had expected the business to grow through franchise and management fees. Instead, growth increasingly came from leasing hotels. Dragisich described the leases as healthy but said the added lease exposure conflicted with Choice's asset-light strategy. The two companies have partnered on distribution since 2018, and Sercotel generated €170 million in revenue in 2025. The exit fee lands alongside Choice's push to recycle capital tied up in real estate: the company recently sold two hotels for about $34 million in estimated net cash proceeds while keeping their franchise contracts.

#6116. China Eastern’s Ex-Chairman Gets 14 Years For $10 Million In Bribes—He Didn’t Follow Xi Jinping’s Instructions

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison in a bribery case involving more than $10 million. The court says Liu Shaoyong sold favors over a period stretching from 2002 through 2023, using positions at both China Eastern and China Southern. He’d left China Eastern in 2022 with a glowing sendoff from the board. Three years later, the Communist Party announced it was investigating him. Corruption can be real, many state bureaucrats are at least a little corrupt Prosecuting often serves a political purpose. A conviction tells us what (who) the government decided to punish. So what’s always interesting in these cases is why this one, and why now. The Shenyang Intermediate People’s Court handed down its verdict on November 3. It found that Liu took more than 67.5 million yuan in bribes (US$10.1 million) in exchange for help with business operations, project contracts, and airline route management. He was also fined 4 million yuan (US$600,000) and disgorgement of his criminal proceeds. Liu admitted guilt at his July 24 trial. The court says it gave him a lighter sentence because he confessed and disclosed bribery facts investigators hadn’t yet uncovered. The party’s earlier disciplinary findings accused him of taking money for hiring favors, improperly holding shares in unlisted companies, helping relatives’ businesses including private equity funds, and accepting payments connected with aircraft leasing and flight management. There were also allegations about gifts, banquets, golf outings, resisting the investigation, and superstitious activities. A former pilot and deputy head of the country’s aviation regulator, Liu went on to lead China Southern before returning to China Eastern in 2008. He was credited with helping turn around both airlines. At China Eastern, his tenure included the Shanghai Airlines merger, entry into SkyTeam, and bringing private investors into parts of the business. The Party Was Already Looking At China Eastern I’ve written about this before with the detention of HNA’s leaders and the government’s takeover of Anbang Insurance. With Liu, there’s a more concrete place to start than guessing which faction he offended. A central party inspection team examined China Eastern from October through December 2023. A February 2025 report covered corruption leads and tightening controls over procurement. Liu was expelled from the party in January 2026. The report puts following Xi Jinping’s instructions, supporting Chinese aircraft, operating at Beijing Daxing, and strengthening party supervision alongside its discussion of corruption. So this was as much about carrying out the party’s priorities as about how he conducted business. The inspection records don’t tell us what finally triggered Liu’s prosecution. They do show specific problems during his tenure, and where running the airline could run into the party’s priorities: Party supervision and insider dealings. In 2015, inspectors reported executives setting up related companies in the same business, extensive use of cargo intermediaries, duplicative rewards for ticket agents, and large numbers of free or discounted tickets. Liu jointly headed the cleanup yet a 2019 inspection again flagged corruption and incomplete fixes. Bringing in private investors while maintaining party control. Liu’s 2017 restructuring of Eastern Air Logistics left China Eastern’s group with 45% ownership, outside investors with 45%, and employees with 10%. A 2020 report flagged shortcomings in integrating party leadership into companies with outside shareholders. It seems like Liu’s efforts at privatization may have provided insufficient Party control. Developing Beijing Daxing even when the airline had commercial reasons to prefer Capital airport. Reporting in 2019 described China Eastern resisting a wholesale move, with concerns about losing business travelers on routes like Beijing–Shanghai. Liu nevertheless publicly outlined plans for around 200 aircraft at Daxing. The government called for more capacity, a better route network, and faster construction of facilities supporting maintenance. By late 2024, party discipline officials were monitoring aircraft deployment and passenger numbers there. Liu resisted building up the Party’s showcase airport. Making Chinese aircraft succeed commercially. Liu was there when China Eastern signed its first firm order for five C919s in March 2021. The airline had also established a subsidiary to operate Chinese regional jets. The C919 only received its type certificate in September 2022, after he left. So Liu didn’t refuse Chinese planes. But the government called for broader route coverage, stronger marketing, and better operating support. They bought the planes but didn’t make the aircraft program work (and they can’t really blame the aircraft, so blame the airlines). Following Xi’s safety instructions. The report published in March 2020 described units giving insufficient attention to important safety and operating issues, failing to escalate major safety matters, and failing to act effectively on identified problems. It called for stronger safety oversight, clearer accountability, and changes involving flight operations, maintenance, and operational control. China Eastern had a crash after the report where the party said Liu’s airline needed to improve. China Eastern flight 5735 crashed in March 2022 and killed 132 people. Liu left the group’s top job four months later. In June 2025, a scholar suggested the crash helped trigger scrutiny of him. Prosecuting Liu enforces discipline over top leadership running Chinese state airlines. I don’t know which patron, rival, or specific transaction made Liu vulnerable. China Eastern’s August 2022 resignation filing said Liu had “faithfully and diligently performed his duties” and thanked him for his “outstanding contributions.” The court now says his bribery stretched through 2023—beyond that farewell. (HT: One Mile at a Time) Topics on this pageChina Eastern AirlinesChinese Communist PartyCommunist partyLiu ShaoyongXi JinpingBeijingBeijing Daxing International AirportChinaChina Southern AirlinesShanghaiShanghai AirlinesSkyTeam+7 more More From View from the Wing

#6115. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

âWe price the product, not the person,â Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. âYour income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay wonât change the price,â he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailerâs AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadnât previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadnât thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. Thereâs something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesnât know how much money you make, whether youâre in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one Iâm growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isnât really the paper. Itâs the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why theyâre paying what theyâre paying. The problem isnât simply higher grocery bills. Itâs the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and heâd rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels arenât, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesnât use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isnât necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

Weâve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, weâre permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.Â

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didnât establish that anyoneâs personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You canât question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarketâs software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. Iâm considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. Itâs one thing to recognize a loyal customer. Itâs another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonaldâs, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmartâs promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and thatâs preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But itâs a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it wonât charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps itâs naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I donât need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.

#6114. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

Airline pricing is once again under scrutiny. Last week, the Federal Trade Commission ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and JetBlue to provide data on how they set fares, as part of a study of whether companies use personal information to set prices.

The FTC sent similar orders to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target and Walmart, seeking data on pricing and, for the gig companies, on worker pay.

The Federal Trade Commission has ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and JetBlue to hand over data on how they set fares, part of a broader study into whether companies use personal information to price goods and services. The airlines have 45 days to respond. The same orders went to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target, and Walmart, with FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson saying the agency intends to scrutinize "opaque" pricing methodology. The inquiry lands as fares have risen sharply this year, largely because of surging jet fuel costs, and as airlines expand their use of AI in pricing. Delta, which told investors in 2024 it was working with the Israeli startup Fetcherr and said last year it was pricing about 3% of domestic routes with AI with a goal of up to 25% by the end of 2025, said it does not use personal data to set fares and has never used, tested, or planned individualized pricing. United referred questions to Airlines for America, which said it welcomes the study and that its carriers do not engage in personalized pricing. JetBlue faces a class action filed in April alleging it uses trackers to set prices dynamically. Roughly a dozen states have proposed laws this year limiting how companies collect and use customer search data, with California, Arizona, Hawaii, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Vermont proposing outright bans on surveillance pricing.
